Circuit: pin 2 -> green wire -> breadboard column 3 -> 82 ohm resistor -> column 6 -> LED anode (longer bent leg); LED cathode in column 8 -> black wire -> GND. This matches the schematic (pin 2 -> resistor -> LED -> GND).
Parts list says 82 ohm; the schematic label says 220 ohm. The parts-list value (82) was kept.
The image's top half is labelled rows j-f; it is mapped to the catalogue's top bank 't' (rows a-e). Only column strips matter, so the circuit is unchanged.
The MKR WiFi 1010 is catalogue type arduino-mkr1000-wifi; pin 2 is port D2 and ground is port GND.

The remaining D8 floating warning is not a real problem for this manual, so I kept the circuit unchanged. The parts list and both the circuit image and the schematic show only a pushbutton between D8 and GND, with no pull resistor. Adding one would break the rule to use exactly the parts the tutorial lists. The board's internal pull-up on D8 (as with INPUT_PULLUP) holds the pin high while the button is open. The sketch uses LowPower.attachInterruptWakeup on pin 8.

The battery's JST PH plug goes into the board's JST socket. The catalogue has no JST port on the MKR WiFi 1010, and port-level edges from the battery leads to BATT and GND were rejected as incompatible kinds. The battery is therefore one port-less 'joined' edge to the board.
The micro-USB power source from the parts list is left out because neither the circuit image nor the schematic shows it.

The pushbutton straddles the breadboard centre gap in column 8. Side 1 is 8b.f and 10b.f, and side 2 is 8t.e and 10t.e. The black wire (GND) goes to 8b.g and the yellow wire (D8) goes to 8t.d, so pressing the button joins D8 to GND.
The catalogue's breadboard banks are named 't' for rows a-e and 'b' for rows f-j. The image draws rows j-f at the top and e-a at the bottom, but the names follow the catalogue.

Fix: the single BATT port was used twice, by the battery + and - leads. The MKR Zero's JST battery connector is now two ports, BATT.+ and BATT.-, so each is used once. The battery + goes to BATT.+ and the battery - goes to BATT.-.
The parts are unchanged from step 1.

The DHT22 sits in breadboard row a, columns 26 to 29, in pin order VCC, SDA (data), NC, GND. The exact holes are read from the image. The red, orange and black jumpers go in row b of the VCC, data and GND columns. The 100nF capacitor goes between columns 26 and 29 in row d. The MKR Zero is not plugged into the breadboard in the image, even though the text says to plug it in. Three jumper wires connect it: VCC to DHT22 power (3.3V), GND to DHT22 ground, and D7 to DHT22 data.
The image is taken as authority. The short blue and yellow strokes are treated as component leads, not extra wires.

The microSD card goes in the MKR Zero slot, modelled as the SD port. The MKR Zero is a new part type because lookup_part did not find it. The 100nF capacitor uses the non-polarised capacitor-22pf type with value=100nF.

The MKR board plugs onto the shield's female headers. The shield catalogue entry has no header ports, so this is a single joined edge with no ports. The internal relay control wiring (pin 1 to relay 1, pin 2 to relay 2) is inside the shield and is not drawn as edges.
The tutorial works with any MKR family board; arduino-mkr1000-wifi was chosen as the generic one.

LED 1 is driven from D3 and LED 2 from D4, as in the sketch. Each LED has a 220 ohm resistor on its anode side. Both cathodes go to the breadboard ground rail (tn), which a jumper wire connects to the MKR GND.
Breadboard hole positions are assumed, since the image is not available as text. The LED cathodes go straight into the ground rail.
Resistor value (220 ohm) and the use of three jumper wires are assumptions.
The 24V lamp and power supply example is illustrative only and is not built. The relays' NO, COM and NC screw terminals are left unconnected.

Fixed the two flagged edges (motor lead to carrier terminal). The carrier's motor screw terminals M1 to M4 were kind 'lug', and a lead cannot join a lug. They are now 'header-socket', the allowed kind for a lead pushed into a socket-style receptacle. The motor leads are clamped in the terminals, hence method=insert and reversible=tool.
Parts are unchanged from step 1.
The MKR Motor Carrier was not found by lookup_part (it returned the unrelated MKR Connector Carrier), so arduino-mkr-motor-carrier was defined as a new part type.
The MKR board mounts on the carrier's header sockets. It is modelled as one joined and electrical edge on MKR_HEADER, with no per-pin mapping, because the tutorial gives none.
The battery goes to the carrier's VIN and GND terminals (the male pins or blue terminal block, which are the same nets). A screw terminal is assumed.
The optional DC motor is on M1+ and M1-. Its two leads are interchangeable, and polarity only sets the spin direction.
The micro USB cable goes to the MKR board's USB port. The computer is not modelled.
The carrier's ON/OFF switch is on the board, so it has no edge. The optional power supply is not built, because it is an alternative to the battery.
Parts are the same as step 1; none added or dropped.
The MKR IoT Carrier sits on the MKR WiFi 1010's header. The board's pins pass through to the carrier, so the join has no specific board port.

The moisture sensor connects to the carrier's A6 Grove connector by the Grove cable. The cable card from lookup_part is a Qwiic-to-Grove adapter (qwiic.* on one end, grove.* on the other). I put the grove.* end on the sensor and the qwiic.* end on the carrier's A6 socket. Grove pin 1 (yellow, SIG) maps to SCL and pin 2 (NC) maps to SDA. The sensor's NC pin and the carrier's A6.NC pin get only joined edges.

Pump polarity: the pump card marks port 1 as the positive (power) pin and port 2 as negative. The pump's + wire goes to relay 1 COM. The USB cable's + wire goes to relay 1 NO. The USB cable's - wire is joined to the pump's - wire, which the tutorial suggests doing in a connector strip. I modelled it as a direct twisted join.

The open-ended USB cable plugs into the adapter's second port. It supplies 5 V to the pump circuit through the relay. The micro-USB cable goes from the first adapter port to the MKR WiFi 1010's USB port and powers the board and carrier.
The text says relay 1 (NO/COM) but the sketch calls opla.Relay2. I followed the text and the circuit description, relay 1.

The plant, the soil and the far end of the watering pipe are not parts in the tutorial's list, so they have no nodes or edges. The pump rests in the water container, and the pipe is pushed onto the pump outlet.
The Arduino Cloud, the phone app and the Wi-Fi are software or services, so they are not in the graph.
Parts are unchanged from step 1.

Each Opta's ETH RJ45 port goes by RJ-45 cable to the Ethernet switch, as in the diagram. The tutorial says the switch is optional and the two Optas can be cabled directly, but its parts list recommends one and the diagram shows it, so it is built.

Each Opta's USB-C port goes by USB-C cable to the computer running the PLC IDE. The diagram draws one computer line branching to both Optas. I modelled it as two cables, one per Opta, using the computer's USB-C and USB-A ports as an assumption.
The usb-cable catalogue type has no ports, so its edges carry no port name.
The optional Modbus TCP compatible device and its field-line link in the diagram are not part of the parts list, so they are omitted.
The status LEDs and relays used in the example are on-board the Opta, so no external LEDs, resistors or wires are used.

Fix: the carrier has no ports in the catalogue, so earlier electrical edges to carrier1 with a null port merged the 12V supply, ground and all signals into one node. Electrical edges now go to the specific MKR Zero pins the carrier routes, and the carrier keeps only joined (mechanical) edges.

Routing through the carrier: A0 carries the moisture signal (gcable1), D0 the water signal (gcable2), D1 the relay signal (gcable3), D12 (SCL) and D11 (SDA) the TWI port (gcable4). Grove VCC goes to mkrzero1 VCC and Grove GND to mkrzero1 GND.

12V path: the supply tip goes to the carrier VIN screw terminal (mkrzero1 VIN). wire7 takes VIN to relay COM and wire5 takes relay NO to the pump. wire6 takes the pump return to GND, and the supply sleeve is GND. The relay is not directly shorted to ground: the pump is in series.

wire7 is not in the tutorial's parts list but is needed to feed the relay COM from 12V, as the Next step text describes. wire3 and wire4 from the earlier draft stay dropped, because a bare wire-end into a barrel-jack socket is not a compatible pair. The supply's tip and sleeve go straight to the carrier screw block, assuming a barrel-to-screw-terminal lead.
Grove cable pin order is 1 = signal (SIG or SCL), 2 = second signal (NC or SDA), 3 = VCC, 4 = GND. The unused NC pin on the analog and digital modules has no electrical edge.
The DPS310 and the OLED share the I2C bus through the I2C hub, which goes to the carrier TWI port. The MKR Zero is a 3.3 V board.

The water sensor hack is two solid wires of different lengths, soldered to two non-adjacent tinned bars. The sensor stays outside the tank and the wires go into the water. The far wire ends are left free.
The pump is a 12V pump, and the tutorial says an electronic valve could replace it. The vase and plant are omitted.

Step 1 parts were correct and are unchanged: Arduino Uno, SCP1000 breakout and 7 hook-up wires, with no breadboard (the circuit image wires the sensor directly to the Arduino).

In the image the breadboard is drawn with rows numbered 1-30 down the side and letters A-J across. Following the catalogue naming, row 24 left half is strip '24t' (A-E) and right half is '24b' (F-J). Row 25 works the same way.

Each button straddles the breadboard centre gap. Side 1 (1.l/1.r) is in the top half (rows f-j, bank 'b'). Side 2 (2.l/2.r) is in the bottom half (rows a-e, bank 't'). The image labels rows J..A from top to bottom, so I mapped rows f-j to bank 'b' and rows a-e to bank 't' to match the catalogue naming.

Button columns, read from the image: S1 1/3, S2 7/9, S3 13/15, S4 19/21, S5 25/27, S6 31/33, S7 37/39. The signal jumper (D2-D8) goes in the right-hand column of the top half. Both are on the button's right-hand column, so the signal and ground sides are on opposite sides of the switch, as in the schematic.

Rail hole numbers are my estimate of the position in the image: groups of 5 holes, with the first hole at column 3. The top rail row next to the blue line is 'tn' and the row next to the red line is 'tp'. The same applies to the bottom rails. The exact hole numbers could be off, but each wire ends on the correct rail.
The image shows the long black jumper joining the top negative rail to the bottom negative rail (tn.48 to bn.48). Arduino GND feeds tn.29, so every button and the potentiometer GND share ground.

The potentiometer's supply comes from the Zero's IOREF pin (3.3 V, as in the schematic and image) through the red jumper to the tp rail, then on to the pot. IOREF is 3.3 V here, which suits the Zero's 3.3 V-only analog input.
Pot VCC and GND are interchangeable (symmetric). The yellow wire from A0 goes to the wiper (SIG).
The Zero's digital-header GND is mapped to the catalogue port GND.1.
No external resistors: the buttons use INPUT_PULLUP in the sketch, and the tutorial lists none.
Correction from the previous version: the parts list has one 220 ohm resistor, so I removed the other three and kept one (r1).

The single resistor sits in the shared ground return, between the MKR GND wire and the breadboard ground rail. Both the white LED cathode and the RGB common cathode go to that rail, so all LED current passes through it. Breadboard placement is my own, because the Fritzing image is not visible as text. The chip straddles the centre gap: pin n is at column 3+n in the top bank (row e) and pin 25-n is in the same column in the bottom bank (row f). Only the top (tp/tn) rails are used for 5V and GND.
Connections follow the sketch comments: CS to pin 10, SDI to pin 11, CLK to pin 13. All A pins and VDD go to +5V. All B pins, GND and VSS go to ground (VSS = 0 V is within the specified range).
Channel i's wiper Wi feeds a 220 ohm resistor, then LED i anode. The LED cathode goes to the ground rail through a jumper. Each resistor is placed in the same breadboard strip as its W pin.
Wire ends on the Arduino are joined to header sockets. Wire ends in the breadboard have both a joined edge and an electrical edge.

Fix: the previous version used a null port on the catalogue 'led-strip' (which has no ports), so all three strip wires collapsed into one node and falsely shorted 5V, GND and D7. strip1 is now a new type 'ws2812-strip-8' with separate pads 5V (the manual's VDC), DIN, GND and DOUT, and no internal connections, so each wire lands on its own pad. The catalogue 'led-strip' was unusable here because it lists no ports.
Wiring: 5V -> strip 5V pad (red); GND -> strip GND pad (black, assumed since the manual only implies it); D7 -> strip DIN (white). DOUT is unused.
No breadboard is used: the manual solders wires directly between the Nano Every, DS3231 module and BME280; all wires are modelled as jumper-wire with both ends soldered.

DS3231MPMB1 is not in the catalogue and lookup found nothing, so it is a new type 'ds3231-rtc' with a GND/VCC/SDA/SCL header on one side and a pass-through header on the other (GND_2/VCC_2/SDA_2/SCL_2), joined internally. The second set of four wires runs from the pass-through side to the BME280.
Nano 3V3 powers the RTC and BME280 (3.3 V part); A4 = SDA (blue), A5 = SCL (yellow).
The USB cable has no catalogue ports, so its end is left unspecified; it plugs into the Nano Every's USB port.
The 3D-printed gnome enclosure is not an electronic part and is omitted.
